Anxiety and related
🌊 Generalised anxiety disorder
Information, not a diagnosisThis page is for information only. Only a professional can assess your situation.
What it is
Everyone feels anxious from time to time. When worry is constant, out of proportion and gets in the way of work, relationships or rest, it may be generalised anxiety disorder (GAD).
Common symptoms
Constant worry about many things (health, work, family, money)
Restlessness, feeling “on edge”
Tiredness and difficulty concentrating
Muscle tension, headaches or digestive problems
Difficulty falling asleep or unrefreshing sleep
Irritability
Myths and facts

Myth: You just need to “stop thinking about it”.
Fact: Anxiety is not a matter of willpower. There are effective treatments and skills that can be learned.

Myth: Anxiety is always bad.
Fact: It is a natural response that protects us. It becomes a problem when it is intense, constant and out of proportion.
When to see a professional
If worry takes up much of your day, you find it hard to function normally, or it has lasted more than six months, talk to your family doctor or a psychologist.
What treatments do clinical guidelines recommend?

Clinical guidelines recommend cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) as the first option; it teaches ways to manage worry. In some cases a professional may also consider medication. The decision is always up to a health professional.
Tips for family and friends
Listen without minimising (“it’s not that bad”).
Avoid agreeing with every fear, but don’t push them to face everything at once either.
Encourage them to ask for help and offer to go with them to the first appointment.

Panic disorder and agoraphobia – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Unexpected panic attacks and fear that they will happen again.
💨 Panic disorder and agoraphobia

A panic attack is an intense wave of fear that peaks within a few minutes. When attacks keep happening and cause constant fear of having another, it is called panic disorder. It can come with avoiding places or situations (agoraphobia).
Palpitations, breathlessness, chest tightness
Dizziness, tingling, sweating or trembling
Feeling unreal or losing control
Fear of “going mad” or dying (even though the attack itself is not dangerous)
Avoiding places where attacks have happened

Myth: A panic attack can cause a heart attack.
Fact: The attack is very unpleasant but not dangerous. If it is your first time or you have doubts, always see a doctor to rule out physical causes.
If you have had a panic attack for the first time, see a doctor to rule out physical causes. If they keep happening or start to limit your life, look for professional help.
CBT with gradual exposure, breathing techniques and reinterpreting bodily sensations is the best-evidenced treatment. A professional may also consider medication.
During an attack, stay calm, speak softly and remind them that it will pass.
Don’t help them avoid everything: avoidance keeps the problem going.
Respect their pace during gradual exposure.
Social anxiety disorder – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Intense fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations.
🫥 Social anxiety disorder
CBT tools for social anxietyExposure hierarchy, thought record and behavioural experiments. Open the tools →
It goes beyond shyness. There is a persistent fear of being judged negatively, which leads to avoiding situations such as public speaking, meeting people or eating in front of others.
Intense fear before and during social situations
Blushing, sweating, trembling, shaky voice
Dreading the situation for days beforehand
Avoiding situations or enduring them with great distress
Self-criticism after an interaction

Myth: It’s just shyness.
Fact: Shyness is a personality trait. Social anxiety causes significant distress and limits life.
When fear stops you studying, working, making friends or taking part in activities you would enjoy.
CBT focused on thoughts and gradual exposure to feared situations. Medication may also be considered.
Don’t force them to face situations all at once.
Celebrate small steps forward.
Don’t tease them or label them “shy”.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and rituals (compulsions) that briefly relieve distress.
🔁 Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)
Obsessions are unwanted thoughts, images or urges that cause distress. Compulsions are repeated behaviours or mental acts done to reduce it. It takes up a lot of time and interferes with daily life.
Fears of contamination, of mistakes, of harming others or of having “terrible thoughts”
Excessive washing, checking, ordering or repeating
Need for symmetry or exactness
Mental rituals (counting, praying, repeating phrases)
Constantly seeking reassurance

Myth: OCD means being very tidy.
Fact: Being tidy is a trait. OCD causes suffering and is not a preference.

Myth: Having intrusive thoughts means you are dangerous.
Fact: They are very common. In OCD they carry disproportionate weight, but they say nothing about who you are.
When rituals take up more than an hour a day, cause distress or limit your life.
CBT with exposure and response prevention is the first-line treatment. Serotonin reuptake inhibitors can help in some cases, always by prescription.
Don’t take part in the rituals or give repeated reassurance: without meaning to, it reinforces them.
Show empathy without judging.
Help them get access to an OCD specialist.
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Lasting reactions after a traumatic experience.
Trauma and grief
⚡ Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
It can appear after living through or witnessing a threatening event (accident, assault, violence, war, sudden loss). The body and mind stay on “alert” for months or years afterwards.
Recurring memories or nightmares
Avoiding related people, places or conversations
Hypervigilance, being easily startled, irritability
Numb emotions or feeling disconnected
Guilt or negative thoughts about yourself or the world

Myth: Only soldiers get PTSD.
Fact: Anyone exposed to trauma can develop it.

Myth: You have to “get over it” on your own.
Fact: People can recover with the right support and treatment.
If, more than a month after a traumatic event, symptoms continue or get worse, or if they affect your life.
Trauma-focused therapies (trauma-focused CBT, EMDR) have the most evidence. They should be delivered by trained professionals.
Don’t pressure them to talk about what happened.
Offer a predictable and safe environment.
Look after yourself too: supporting someone with trauma is draining.
Depression – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Persistent sadness or loss of interest that affects daily life.
Mood
🌧️ Depression
If you are in danger nowCall 112 or 024 (free, 24 h). You don’t have to face this alone.
Depression is more than feeling sad for a few days. It is a mood disorder that affects how you feel, think and act, and lasts weeks or months.
Sadness or emptiness most of the day
Loss of interest or pleasure in activities
Changes in appetite, weight or sleep
Tiredness and lack of energy
Feelings of guilt or worthlessness
Difficulty concentrating or making decisions
Thoughts of death or of not wanting to live (see the urgent help section)

Myth: It is weakness or lack of willpower.
Fact: It is a health problem with biological, psychological and social causes.

Myth: If you have a “good” life, you can’t be depressed.
Fact: Depression can appear without any obvious reason.
If symptoms last more than two weeks and affect your life. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, ask for help immediately (112 / 024).
Depending on severity: psychotherapy (CBT, behavioural activation, interpersonal therapy), antidepressants or a combination. Exercise, a sleep routine and social support help as a complement.
Listen without trying to “cheer them up” by force.
Suggest small shared activities, without demanding.
Take any comment about not wanting to live seriously and ask them directly, calmly.
Bipolar disorder – symptoms and help | Psicòleg
Alternating episodes of elevated mood (mania/hypomania) and depression.
🎢 Bipolar disorder
It is marked by pronounced changes in mood and energy. Episodes of euphoria or intense irritability alternate with depressive episodes, with periods of stability in between.
Periods of high energy, little sleep and lots of activity
Grandiose ideas, rapid speech, impulsivity
Spending sprees or risky behaviour
Depressive periods with sadness and lack of energy

Myth: These are normal mood swings.
Fact: Bipolar episodes are more intense and longer-lasting and affect functioning.

Myth: With medication you no longer need therapy.
Fact: Psychoeducation and routine are pillars of treatment.
See a psychiatrist if you have noticed periods of unusually high energy and activity or marked mood changes.
Usual treatment combines mood stabilisers prescribed by psychiatry with psychoeducation and regular routines (sleep, schedules). Medication should not be stopped without consulting the professional.
Learn to recognise the warning signs of a new episode.
Avoid arguing about ideas during a manic episode.
